Q: click) passing iteration variable and [class.selected] passing function A:

This is an example of parent-child communication in angular2.

When you are using (click)='clicked(myProduct)' event, what essentially you are doing is emitting the value of the selected product using @ouput onProductSelected property as shown here :

this.onProductSelected.emit(product);
$event` here would be equivalent to `#myProduct.value

When any event gets executed, angular2's change detections kicks-in; checking all the template expression values. It then updates the property binding as per value changes. now everytime value of myProduct changes, the property binding [class.selected] need to get updated , hence isSelected method gets called.

Q: how can we join this two table results in to one A:

We don't have an abundance of sample data to sanity check with, but it seems to me that the mostly cause of the problem is insufficient grouping. If you are going to present data confined by user and date, then the GROUP BY should be by user and date. Maybe it will be easiest or clearest if you generate two subqueries that share that GROUP BY logic, then JOIN the payloads of those subqueries in a parent query. Below is my untested advice.

public function getTotalPriceAndWinningByUserForDateRange(
    string $start_date,
    string $end_date
): array {
    $purchases = $this->db
        ->select('DATE(b.date) date, bd.agent_name user_id')
        ->select_sum('bd.profit', 'total_profit')
        ->join('bill_details bd', 'bd.bill_id = b.id', 'left')
        ->where('b.date >=', $start_date . ' 00:00:00')
        ->where('b.date <=', $end_date . ' 23:59:59.999') 
        ->group_by(['DATE(b.date)', 'bd.agent_name'])
        ->get_compiled_select('bills b');

    $winning = $this->db
        ->select('DATE(ar.date) date, ar.user_id')
        ->select_sum('(ar.total_price + ar.total_dc)', 'winning')
        ->where('ar.date >=', $start_date . ' 00:00:00')
        ->where('ar.date <=', $end_date . ' 23:59:59.999')
        ->group_by(['DATE(ar.date)', 'ar.user_id'])
        ->get_compiled_select('assigned_result ar');

    return $this->db
        ->select('date, user_id agent_name, p.total_profit, w.winning')
        ->join("($winning) w", 'date,user_id', 'left')
        ->get("($purchases) p")
        ->result();
}

Q: Profiling .NET applications with Stopwatch A:

First thing's first: your results are not at all surprising. If you used a commercial profiler, you would see something similar: your program will take a lot longer to run when it is being profiled than when it is not. The more granular you set the profiler, the longer you can expect it to take. When you consider that statements like "i > 1" and "i--" will likely be executed as single processor instructions, it becomes obvious why profiling the execution time of a particular line can take a lot longer than executing the line itself.

The fact that profiling is increasing the overall running time of your program should not be a concern; as several others have mentioned, what matters is not the absolute amount of time the program runs, but comparing the running time of the individual parts against each other to find the bottleneck. But there is another concern. Stopwatch will use the high frequency timer from the underlying OS if one is available; but even that may not be high enough. The high frequency timer on my Windows 7 64-bit i5-2400 (Quad core 3.10 GHz) ticks 3,020,556 times per second. That sounds like a lot; but at that rate, the processor could execute a thousand instructions between ticks. That means if you are trying to measure the time it takes to execute a single instruction, you are either going to way under or way overshoot.

You would be better off profiling at the method level. Even then you will run into frequency issues, particularly if you have small well-factored methods. But the results will be more reliable than at the line level; and once you have identified the method that is causing the bottleneck, you can examine it directly to determine how to optimize it to perform better.

All of this leaves aside the many caveats that go along with performance profiling in general, which would be outside the scope of this post. Make sure you do additional research on the subject to understand how you should interpret whatever results you get. As a quick example, your profiling may reveal that the majority of the time in your program is being spent in a particular method; but does that mean that the method itself is the problem, or that other methods are calling it too often? Answering that kind of question is where the real difficulty in profiling lies.

Q: How do you find the disk size of a Postgres / PostgreSQL table and its indexes A:

Based on @aib's answer and @Ciges's improvement on materialized view, this will additionally include partitioned table as in the value p of pg_class.relkind. Also turn nesting sub queries into CTE.

WITH all_tables AS (
    SELECT s.oid::regnamespace schema,
           c.oid::regclass "table",
           s.oid::regnamespace || '.' || c.oid::regclass schema_table
    FROM pg_catalog.pg_namespace s
    JOIN pg_catalog.pg_class c ON c.relnamespace = s.oid
    WHERE c.relkind IN ('r', 'p', 'm')
      AND s.nspname NOT IN ('information_schema', 'pg_catalog')
), pretty_sizes AS (
    SELECT *,
           pg_table_size(schema_table) AS table_size,
           pg_indexes_size(schema_table) AS indexes_size,
           pg_total_relation_size(schema_table) AS total_size
    FROM all_tables
    ORDER BY total_size DESC
)
SELECT schema, "table",
       pg_size_pretty(table_size) AS table_size,
       pg_size_pretty(indexes_size) AS indexes_size,
       pg_size_pretty(total_size) AS total_size
FROM pretty_sizes

Q: Ruby Email validation with regex A:

you can just do something in this regard:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  validates :email,
    presence: true,
    format: { with: URI::MailTo::EMAIL_REGEXP }
end
